utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence will today present its opening statement and put its case regarding the issues of fact and law raised in the indictment against the accused, Mr. Milan Martic. The Defence will draw attention to those fundamentals and the Defence standpoints which will show that the charges in the indictments are not well founded, that they constitute a view of highly complex military multi-national state and other relations over a five-year period on the territory of a former European country, Yugoslavia, and that the Prosecution has taken a selective view of these facts and events, extracted them from their context, and failed to establish causal links. At the outset, the Defence wants to point out that the Prosecution is mentioning a third of the territory of the former Socialist Republic of Croatia, which at that time was inhabited by Serbs as the indigenous population, and considerable parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the context of the overall Yugoslav crisis, to which all documents of the United Nations testify. However, the Prosecution sees this territory, about one-third of Croatia, a considerable part of Bosnia, in a context severed from the territory of the rest of Yugoslavia, the other events and influences and attempts to construct their case concerning a so-called joint criminal enterprise based on witness testimony and documents. The Defence will begin with a chronological overview of the events that took place in that period of time on that territory. What is characteristic of this period of time relevant for the indictment, and formally this is the period from 1991 to 1995, is the emergence of certain political parties of the territory of the former Yugoslavia and the then federal unit of Croatia. In early 1989, in Croatia, the Croatian Democratic Union was established headed by Mr. Franjo Tudjman. Until that time, this had not been a political party, and could not have been registered under the regulations. It was registered as a party only later and this was done pursuant to the regulations in force. A year later, on the territory of the SAO Krajina or Croatia the Serb Democratic Party was also registered. In 1990, therefore, at the beginning of that year, new parties emerged on the territory of the then Yugoslav Republic of Croatia in circumstances where the Yugoslav crisis, as an issue of state and of international significance, under international law, starts to culminate. The Prosecution case is that the emergence of certain nationalist parties led to all the evil mentioned in the indictment. However, the emergence of these parties was only a very small part of the overall mosaic of political events and tendencies and aspirations emerging in Yugoslavia at the time. In 1990, just as had happened 50 years previously, there was only one state, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on that territory. I will refer to it as Yugoslavia further, and by this I mean the entire territory of that state. In 1990, 1991 and until mid-1992, under international law, there was no doubt that there was only one legal entity, only one internationally recognised state, and that was precisely Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia was one of the 45 founder members of the United Nations. In 1990 and 1991, it was a member of the United Nations and, in all respects, its behaviour and actions were in line with the principles of the OSCE, and it was a well-respected member of the international community; so neither in 1990 or in 1991 were any of the federal units of Yugoslavia internationally recognised states. These were administrative units within the Yugoslav federation and they were not legal entities on the international level. Why is the Defence raising these issues? Because the events that were to take place and lead to war and disaster can briefly be described in a single sentence. This was the attempt of certain Yugoslav federal units, primarily Slovenia and Croatia to, in contravention of the provisions of the Yugoslav constitution and international law, secede from Yugoslavia. They wanted to do this and they carried this out at any cost. This process of destroying the Yugoslav state started when these separatist demands were put forward by Croatia and Slovenia as early as 1990. At the level of the Yugoslav state, and the federation, negotiations were held at Presidency level to find a possible solution to these problems. No one in the federal top leadership of Yugoslavia wanted war or prepared for war. Otherwise there would have been no talks and no negotiations. In all this it is important to bear in mind one more fact. Until 1990 on the territory of Yugoslavia, there was total peace. All the members of the Yugoslav federation were equal in status and in all their rights. All the members of the Yugoslav federation, according to the Yugoslav constitution and their own constitutions, participated on a footing of full equality in the functioning of the Yugoslav federation. Your Honours, you have heard many times of the Yugoslav Presidency. This was the so-called collective head of state. I think it is hard to find another such example in the federal practice of any country in the world. Of course, this is a positive example. It's a positive exception, because it was the result of endeavours in the Yugoslav constitution and the constitutions of the federal member republics of Yugoslavia to have each of them represented in the organ referred to as the collective head of state. Therefore, under the constitution, each republic provided one member so that the six republics and two autonomous provinces within Serbia, under the Yugoslav constitution provided eight representatives and these eight representatives were the collective head of state. To secure full equality, when decisions had to be made at state level, these members of the collective Presidency were rotated every year so that one year the Slovenian representative was the president of the Presidency, followed by the one from Macedonia and so on. I won't mention each one of the federal units. The constitution of Yugoslavia also provided for the possibility of individual federal units becoming independent and separating from Yugoslavia. The status of the federal units was highly favourable for them. This possibility, however, was dependent on compliance with the constitutional procedure, which required the agreement of all the other members. Of course, it's easy to say what the secessionist leaderships of Croatia and Slovenia said, that this was simply an obstacle in their way, but there can be no democratic order in a state if one of six members of a federation can do whatever it wants. The Yugoslav constitution envisaged the right to self-determination and even secession, but this had to be done pursuant to a joint decision made by all the federal units. In 1990, the leaderships of Croatia and Slovenia did not wish to acquire such consent. They saw this as unacceptable. Those two leaderships, those of Croatia and Slovenia, and those two Yugoslav federal units wanted independence immediately and at any cost, even at the cost of war. The most influential Croatian politician in that period, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, the president of Croatia and the president of the HDZ, which was the most influential party in Croatia, publicly and clearly stated, as early as in May 1992, openly, at a rally before 100.000 people in the centre of Zagreb, "our assessment was that independence can be won only through war. There would have been no war had we not wanted it." Mr. Tudjman went on to explain in March or rather, May, 1992, that they had conducted political negotiations, these were negotiations among the Yugoslav republics, about a possibility solution, but we were preparing for war. And how were they preparing for war? That is a question which the Defence is deeply convinced the Chamber will have to find an answer to in order to reach a just verdict. Some elements are already before the Chamber, based on the evidence presented by the Prosecution. The Prosecution expert, Theunens, during cross-examination, confirmed that the leadership of Croatia called upon the population of Croatia to rebel and another Prosecution witness confirmed that this was an armed rebellion. A great deal of evidence presented during the Prosecution case points to armed activities and armed rebellion. Protocol 2 of the Geneva Conventions envisages what a state should do when there is an armed rebellion. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, under international law, was duty bound to deal with this armed rebellion and to deal with it as an internal issue. It was duty-bound to suppress this rebellion. This was also provided for by the Yugoslav constitution and all federal laws. The armed forces of any country can be used for such a purpose, including the armed forces of Yugoslavia. The Prosecutor claims that the activities of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, the federal armed force, constituted aggression against the federal units. Of course, I do not believe that my learned friend is not familiar with the elementary norms of international law and he must also be familiar with the Yugoslav constitution. This is, however, an attempt to construct a fictional account of a so-called joint criminal enterprise. The essence of this fabrication is that the activity of the federal armed force, following orders from the head of state to suppress an armed rebellion, constituted an aggression on their own country, Croatia and Slovenia. This is what the Prosecutor is claiming. How this happened I will demonstrate later on during my opening statement. I will now go back to year 1990. At that point, when we know there was a political crisis in the territory of Yugoslavia, as displayed in the political demands of certain federal units that are mutually opposed, some of them wanted to leave Yugoslavia and to become independent, such as Slovenia and Croatia, others wanted to stay within Yugoslavia, such as Bosnia, Macedonia, Serbia and Montenegro, wherefore in the political negotiations in that year 1990, various political options were put on the table, there occurred the sudden introduction of the multi-party system in Yugoslavia, national parties emerged, nation-based parties whose main determinant is a membership that belongs to one ethnic group. The very name Croatian Democratic Union shows that it is a Croatian national party. The Serb Democratic Party shows in its name that it is primarily a party of the Serbs. Of course, it is envisaged in the charter that anybody can become a member but the essence of those parties is that they are national by orientation, and under the circumstances in 1990, the first multi-party elections are organised in Croatia. Several parties were running in those elections and examining and cross-examining witnesses before the trial Chamber we have mentioned all of them and we will not repeat all of their names now. What is important for the first half of 1990 is the emergence of the Croatian Democratic Union, its rise as the most important Croatian party, and its victory at the elections in April 1990. It won 41 per cent of the votes and thanks to the majority election system, it won two-thirds of the seats in the parliament called Sabor in Croatia. What is important in order to gain a full picture of the events of that time is to understand the political platform of that party. The Croatian Democratic Union, led by Franjo Tudjman, had as its objective an independent Croatian state of the Croatian people. Croatia as a state of the Croatian people. The Serb Democratic Party also ran in those 1990 elections, nationalist party, as the Prosecutor called it, led by Jovan Raskovic. Although this party qualified to become a participant in the elections meeting all the requirements for registration and other criteria. Would it have been possible at that time to register a party in Croatia if it expressed nationalism in any form, especially Serbian nationalism at that time; this party, however, was registered. So under those circumstances, in the beginning of 1990, when the first multi-party elections were being held and when the Croatian Democratic Union won a landslide victory to become the most important party in the parliament and in all of Croatia, the participation of the Serb Democratic Party led by Jovan Raskovic is treated in the Prosecution case as part of the joint criminal enterprise or its preparation. So at that point, when those first multi-party elections were taking place in Croatia, with the participation of the Serb Democratic Party, the then federal unit of Croatia had around four and a half million population, including 581.000 people who had declared themselves as Serbs in the census. According to official data from the census of that year, Serbs accounted for 12 per cent of Croatian population. Out of 581.000 Serbs at the first elections in Croatia, a very small number voted for the Serb Democratic Party. The Serb Democratic Party won only in Knin plus another one or two municipalities perhaps. The greatest majority of the Croat Serb population voted for another party, the party of Ivica Racan, the former Croat communist who had transformed the Croatian Communist Party into a new party, Party of Democratic Changes. Why am I mentioning this? All this would be irrelevant if it had not been turned upside down by the Prosecution. And how did the Prosecution do that? They were trying to represent -- misrepresent completely the then political situation in Croatia when those first multi-party elections were held, there were two peoples, two nations, in Croatia; according to the constitution itself, Croatia was defined as the state of Croat and Serb people in Croatia, not Serb people from Serbia but Serb people from Croatia. And that was the solution, the constitutional arrangement, that had prevailed for the previous 50 years, from the end of World War II. And the reason why Serbs had that status in Croatia is that before World War II, that is until 1941, there had been a million of them in Croatia. So on the territory of the then Independent State of Croatia, a million Serbs were killed in a terrible genocide. Those are the available data, 700.000 were killed a horrific concentration camp called Jasenovac and the overall estimate of Serbs killed is one million. On the territory of Croatia, 50 years after the Second World War, 581.000 Serbs were resident, and that provision in the Croatian institution was a reference to that people who was killed through genocide in World War II. When the Prosecution explain in their case the political events and political aspirations, they do admit to the horrible suffering of World War II, but in a cynical way; cynical because that is a crime with no statute of limitations. We saw the map of the Independent State of Croatia and we saw that it was the only country in Hitler's Europe at the time where there was a concentration camp outside Germany, a horrible concentration camp. And the Prosecutor says, "But Serbian population did suffer a genocide in the past but its fears in exaggerated so since its fears were exaggerated, somebody instigated Serb nationalism and then out of that Serb nationalism the Serbs moved on to create a greater Serbia, kill Croats, et cetera." That is the Prosecution case. The Prosecution, by the way, disclosed a great number of documents to the Defence that testify to the prevailing political situation in that year, 1990, in the territory of Yugoslavia. So we cannot really say that the Prosecution does not know the situation well. The Prosecution has to know that situation by virtue of their job, and the Prosecution disclosed written evidence which shows the writing of Der Spiegel magazine of 16th April 1990, referring to the elections in Croatia, and I quote, "The greatest chances of success at these elections are in the hands of the Croatian Democratic Union, an extremist group that openly dreams of a Greater Croatia, has territorial claims on the neighbouring Bosnia-Herzegovina," and I now come from the most important point, "And spreads fanatical hatred of Serbs." So on the eve of the elections in Croatia, where the Croatian Democratic Union was victorious, led by Franjo Tudjman, this Croatian Democratic Union was a party which, according to this German publication was spreading fanatical hatred for the Serbs. We will show that this election campaign of the Croatian Democratic Union and all the other Croatian parties which defined themselves as Croatian, were based on hatred of Yugoslavia and intolerance of a part of the population in their own republic. It was not hatred directed against Serbs in Serbia or Serbs in the United States. It was hatred directed against 12 per cent of their own population. The Prosecution did touch upon this election campaign and we have parts of Mr. Tudjman's speech recorded on paper and on video and audio tape, a speech held before these elections in April 1990, namely on the 24th of February, in a big hall, congress hall, Vatroslav Lisinski, where he says that the wartime Independent State of Croatia is not only a quisling creature in the expression of -- but also the expression of historic aspirations of the Croatian people. To call that fascist state of Croatia, which was a Hitler satellite during the war and as such declared war on Britain and the United States and continued in that war until 1945, a state whose troops were on the eastern front near Stalingrad and a state which, by the way, killed a million Serbs, to call that state on the eve of 1990 elections in Croatia an expression of historic aspirations of the Croatian people ... However, Mr. Tudjman did precisely that, that sentence rang the alarm bell in the ears of all Serbs. It sent shivers down their spines. It froze their blood. Foreign press was writing about nationalist Croatia at that time. However, that can be a matter of political struggle and political moment. But the elections passed, the parties that vied for political power won as many votes as they won, and it was important for life to go on. What happened then? The first enactments passed by the new Croatian authorities were those amending the Croatian institution, to stipulate that Croatia is a state of Croats only. Passing amendments that deprived the Serbs of their status of people and reduced them to a national minority. Their script is banned and the old wartime chequerboard flag of Croatia is reintroduced, the notorious flag, in red and white. We heard a number of Prosecution witnesses speak about that flag. It is of course an indisputable right of the people in power in any Yugoslav federal unit to decide what their flag would be. However, in this case, it was the combination of choice of moment and choice of method. At that moment, Serbs were very anxious, fearsome [as interpreted], Yugoslavia was facing threat of break-up, Croatia was openly threatening to separate from Yugoslavia and the Serbs started to react through their political representatives, in a purely political way. A party is formed, it takes part in elections, they won a limited number of votes, and then Serbs, who until then were members of other parties, as a result of violations of the rights of Serb people and Serb parties, changed their affiliation and joined the Serb political party. The objective of the victorious party, however, was to expel one-third of its own population. The Prosecution, however, claims that it was the other way round, that the Serbs wanted to create a greater Serbia by expelling one-third of Croats from their territory. That is absurd. Why would they do that? The Prosecutor does not say so in so many words, but it is claimed that it is purely because Serbs hate Croats. Let us expel all the Croats and create an independent Krajina. When Serbs organised political parties in the territory of Croatia, they, who were Croat citizens, found out about amendments proposed by Tudjman, they wrote letters of protests and their own counterproposals which were rejected. The Serb population was a minority at that moment, a small minority, with a very small political influence. Under those circumstances, when the Croatian parliament does not wish to accept a single amendment proposed by the Serb side, political rallies are organised in Croatia. For instance, the rally in a place called Srb on the 25th of July 1990, attended by 20.000 Serbs from that area. The Prosecution refers to this as the first step in what will follow, but disregards the amendments that had been passed and the reason why those changes were instilling fear in the Serb population, the fear of evil repeating itself. The Serbs responded to what was happening in the parliament of Croatia with the rally of the 25th of July 1990 in Srb. At the same time the chequerboard emblem was being introduced in the Croatian parliament. The Serbs were active politically. They issued a declaration on the sovereignty of the Serb people. According to the Prosecutor, this declaration is also part of the joint criminal enterprise. However, they are overlooking the fact that under the Croatian constitution valid until that point, the Serb population did have the status of a constituent nation. This document issued in Srb was of a declarative nature. The Serbs had already been a nation for 50 years and at that rally, they confirmed this. They say, "We are a nation and that's how we want to be treated." The Serb National Council is therefore established at that time and they organised a referendum to deal with these issues. In conditions where the Croatian and Slovenian political leaderships wanted to secede from Yugoslavia at any cost, this behaviour of the frightened Serbs in Croatia was something that was perhaps even grist to the mill of the Croatian leadership. A referendum as a form of political expression was provided for in the constitutions of both Croatia and Yugoslavia and still is today. The Serbs therefore held a referendum starting on the 19th of August about their autonomy and their status as a nation in Croatia. On the 17th of August, the Croatian authorities prohibited this referendum and sent Croatian policemen to prevent the holding of this referendum and to disarm the police stations on those territories inhabited by a majority Serb population, in Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and other places. Prosecution witnesses have testified to this. All this has been established beyond dispute from Prosecution witnesses. The decision of the Croatian government to ban the referendum which was issued on the 17th of August and their sending policemen to disarm those police stations caused total panic among the Serbs. An alarm was sounded in Knin, a state of war was declared, and barricades were erected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who declared the state of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The president of the municipal assembly of Knin, the late Mr. Babic. As the president of the Knin municipal assembly, Mr. Babic issued a decision on the 17th of August 1990 to declare a state of war in Knin, and an air raid siren was sounded. The population was warned over the radio of the possible arrival of Croatian policemen and, of course, the response was quite logical and natural. The Serb population set up log barricades on the roads. Barricades by their very name are clearly used to prevent movement along a road, and in the context in which they were erected, it's evident that they were intended to prevent the arrival of armed Croatian policemen. This was an attempt to erect a physical obstacle on the road and therefore to protect the population and to make the people feel safer. The Prosecutor says these barricades were used for purposes of attack, aggression, joint criminal enterprise. Although he presented part of the book written by Mr. Jovic, the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, saying that the planes of the Yugoslav air force made helicopters of the Croatian MUP turn back. They had set out from Lucko in Croatia to intervene with weapons in Knin. It would have been a massacre, Your Honours. The Prosecutor brought witnesses who we will not comment on, who explained that the barricades erected on the roads were an obstacle only to the Croats. They were erected in order to imperil the Croatian population. This would be ridiculous. It would be humorous were it not so terrible, this total inversion of the meaning of these barricades. The Defence will show that object the 20th or 21st of August, three days before the barricades were erected, or after they were erected, at one of these barricades several buses were stopped travelling from Drnis to Knin, and there were men with weapons inside going to take over the police station in Knin and it was only the behaviour of the people on the barricades that prevented the massacre which could have taken place over the Croatian policemen who ran into an ambush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm beginning to worry, Mr. Milovancevic, you sound now like you are testifying. I'm not suggesting that what you have been saying is strictly according to what I expect an opening statement should be. You've been sounding all the time like you're making a closing argument but now you seem to be testifying. Can I suggest that you try to stick to opening statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Your Honour? The Defence has dwelt in detail on these facts because these are key points on the basis of which the Prosecutor builds his case of a joint criminal enterprise. The chronology of events that followed goes to deny this case. The Defence will show that the meaning, both in political and military terms, of these events was quite different from the meaning ascribed to them by the Prosecutor. If anything were to be selected as the most significant fact in that year, it was the setting up of barricades in Knin. The result of the referendum at which the Serbs voted in favour of their autonomy and then the decision of the 21st of December 1990 on the establishing of the SAO Krajina. As the Defence will demonstrate through witnesses, the Serbs, in holding a referendum like the previous rally at Srb, did what Mr. Raskovic explained in great detail at the Srb rally. He said "the goal of our political activity is not to create a greater Serbia. It's not to take up weapons. It's not to enter into a conflict with the remaining population in Croatia. We are simply responding to the claims made by the state leadership of Croatia that what is happening on the territory of the Krajina is being done only by a handful of bandits and that the majority of the Serb population in these area does not share their opinions." That's why the referendum was organised and carried out, to show that the Serbs were in favour of autonomy. It was held from the 19th of August to the 2nd of September and pursuant to that referendum, the Serb Autonomous Province of Krajina was promulgated. We will show why it was on the 21st of December 1990 that the SAO Krajina was promulgated. Its very name, Serb Autonomous Province of Krajina, shows quite clearly that this was a province within the Republic of Croatia. This was autonomy within Croatia. Whereas the Prosecutor tries to portray this as an attempt to have the Krajina secede from Croatia. There is no dispute that in the Statute of the SAO Krajina, it was stated that the Krajina was part of Croatia and that Croatian legislation applied on its territory. The fact that this happened on the 21st of December 1994 [as interpreted] is used by the Prosecutor to show that the joint criminal enterprise started as early as that. He is overlooking the fact that on the very next day, the 22nd of December, the new Croatian constitution was enacted, under which the Serbs were no longer a constituent nation but a national minority. I am mentioning all this, Your Honours, to show the link between these events. The political actions of the Serbs in Croatia were, as a rule, a response to the actions of the Croatian authorities, which were about to happen. That's why a day before the constitution under which the Serbs were no longer a constituent nation in Croatia, the Serbs issued their own document of the 21st of December promulgating their autonomous province. The Defence will show that the political aspirations of the Croatian leadership to secede from Yugoslavia were implemented on two levels, through political activities seeking support abroad for such demands, and internal activities, that is preparations for war. The Croatian federal unit of Croatia was preparing for war with its own country. The Defence will show that in September, October, and November 1990, there was illegal import of weapons into Croatia. The well-known film about Martin Spegelj, the commander of the new Croatian army, shows this. He is talking to Boljkovac, the Croatian Minister of the Interior in that film. In any case, what happened in 1991 represents a huge acceleration of the Yugoslav crisis with mounting secessionist demands on the part of Croatia and Slovenia, the attempts of the Yugoslav leadership to keep this crisis within a political framework rather than a military one and the taking of a number of steps to avoid military conflicts. This acceleration of political events is again represented by the Prosecutor as alleged evidence of a joint criminal enterprise. The fact that the Serbs established the SAO Krajina on the 21st of December 1990 is taken by the Prosecutor as a prime piece of evidence testifying to such an enterprise, whereas it was quite possible, under the Yugoslav and Croatian constitutions, to declare autonomy pursuant to a referendum which is precisely the way this happened. But the Prosecution construes it differently. In the SAO Krajina new government was elected, with Mr. Babic at its head and on the 4th of January it appointed ministers and Mr. Martic was then appointed a secretary of the interior and this again is seen by the Prosecutor as evidence of a joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, in January, February and March, all the way until August 1991, on the territory of Yugoslavia, there was no war. It was a state with all its state organs. We can view them as regular or irregular but there were police stations, chiefs of police, both in Croatia and in Slovenia and in every Yugoslav republic in every town and village. The appointment of one man, Mr. Martic, to be secretary of the police is not evidence that there was a joint criminal enterprise. It's only evidence showing that the political leadership of Krajina assessed Mr. Martic as being a person suitable for the job. That's all it shows. And this was done in accordance with the legislation in place at the time. However, events took a completely different course, as we will demonstrate. On the 9th of January 1991, the Presidency of Yugoslavia issued a decision on the disarming of paramilitary formations, all paramilitary formations in Yugoslavia, including Slovenia and Croatia. The leaderships of Slovenia and Croatia refused to implement this decision. On the 25th of January, in Belgrade, the Presidency of Yugoslavia, after their order that paramilitary formations be disbanded was rejected, issued a decision on the demobilisation of all reserve police units. That is when the video footage of Martin Spegelj is broadcast on television, causing the whole public to go into a state of shock. Even that decision of the Presidency, to demobilise reserve police forces is not enforced by the state of Croatia, and we will show that as well. It was not an ordinary mobilisation of the reserve police forces. That video footage had, by that time, shown that 54.000 automatic rifles had been imported, smuggled in from Hungary and we will show that the mobilisation of reserve police in Croatia was a way to create a new Croatian army. At any rate, it is indubitable that the leadership of the federal units of Croatia and Slovenia were refusing to implement the decisions of the collective head of state, the Presidency of Yugoslavia. On a parallel track with this conduct towards the federal state, on the 21st of February 1991, Croatia passed a decision rendering null and void all federal legislation in the territory of Croatia, thereby stepping out and excluding itself from the constitutional order of the country. On the 28th of February, the Serbian -- the Autonomous District of Krajina responds with an enactment on disassociation from Croatia, and this again is treated by the Prosecution as an element of joint criminal enterprise, which is contrary to all logic. Alongside with this failure to respect federal legislation, the situation in Croatia is growing ever more tense, and on the 2nd of March 1991, the population of Pakrac clashed with the Croatian authorities and police. That caused great anxiety among Croatian Serbs in general, whereas the Prosecution is trying to convince us that this was an attempt to encourage Croatian Serbs to armed insurgency. This is how the first armed clash occurred, orchestrated and stage-managed by the new authorities of Croatia. It was a crime against peace. After this first clash, of the 2nd of March 1991 in Pakrac, the Presidency of Yugoslavia, as the collective head of state, tried to decide on the proposal of the Federal Secretariat for Defence to introduce a state of emergency that would enable the federal army to mobilise people, to mobilise men, in order to implement the decision of the Presidency, to disarm paramilitary units. The Defence will show that that decision was not passed because the Presidency voted four versus four. The representatives of Slovenia, Croatian, Bosnia and Macedonia, those republics that later seceded from Yugoslavia voted against authorising the Yugoslav People's Army to disarm paramilitary units. And after that, events begin to spiral. The next clash occurred on the 31st of March, between local Serbs and the Croatian police in Plitvica. Two people were killed, 20 wounded. The federal police were sent in to separate the conflicting sides. And already on the 2nd May, in Borovo Selo a new clash occurred again between armed Croatian police and the local population, in which 17 members of the Croatian armed forces were killed -- sorry, 13, not 17. That is already a time in 1991 when events are getting out of political control. Near Benkovac, the chief of the police station was killed in Polaca near Benkovac which caused great indignation among the Croats, and this indignation gave rise to mass vandalisation of Serb property on the 3rd of May, and we will call witnesses to speak about this. Whereas on the 5th of May in Trogir, Franjo Tudjman called the Croat people to insurgency. That was confirmed by more than one witness, and the Defence will show it. And after this call to armed insurgency, already on the 6th of May 1991 in Split, huge disorders occurred in the streets and one soldier was killed, another was wounded. Were these accidents? No. They were an overture into the referendum on the independence of Croatia that was scheduled for the 19th of May 1991. At that referendum, the Croat population of Croatia voted en masse for independence. The Serb citizens of Croatia did not vote. This -- in response to this referendum, the leadership of SAO Krajina scheduled its own referendum for the 12th of May 1991, where the Serb population voted in favour of staying within Yugoslavia, remaining a part of Yugoslavia, and the way this question was formulated is again treated by the Prosecution as evidence of a joint criminal enterprise. However, Your Honours, it is the right and even the duty of all populations to be loyal to their federal state, and that was what the Serb population in Croatia voted for on the 12th of May. When the Croatian referendum passed and the majority of Croats voted for secession of Croatia, already on the 28th of May 1991, Franjo Tudjman inspected the new Croatian army at a stadium in Zagreb, the new army was called ZNG, the Croatian home guard. This is a fact that the Prosecution seems to disregard. On the territory of a still-existing state, a new army is proclaimed that is preparing to go to war with the regular army. The Prosecution treats the proclamation of independence of Croatia as a perfectly regular act. He does not see it as evidence of intention to break up the existing regular state. Secession as such is seen in the international community, and international law, as a festering wound on the body of the world. However, it is precisely secession that Slovenia and Croatia were bent on and they proclaimed it on the 15th of June in 1991. The Prosecution treats the refusal of the Yugoslav state to accept this secession as proof of aggression against its own constituent members. Unbelievable but true. And before we go on our first break in one minute, at the time when all this is happening in Slovenia and Croatia, the Presidency is presided over by a Slovene, representative of the state which took such a decision to secede. The next president was Stjepan Mesic, again a representative of a republic that decided to secede. There was a representative of Macedonia, a representative of Bosnia. So the collective head of state was functioning in complete accordance with the constitution at the time when these decisions on secession were adopted, and the federal Prime Minister, a Croat, Ante Markovic, proclaimed that these enactments, these proclamations of independence were unconstitutional already the next day, the 26th of June 1991, and the federal government sent 2000 troops to restore order at the Slovene borders. Your Honours, perhaps this would be a convenient moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. We will then take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before the break, we left off with the events of end June 1991. Of course, all those were things of common knowledge and the Prosecutor does note that in the indictment, that at that time two republics enacted proclamations on secession and conflicts started. We also know what was going on in Slovenia at the time. What is important to point out at this moment is that the acts of Slovenia and Croatia were unlawful, violent, illegal, and that the federal government of Yugoslavia, headed by a Croat, Ante Markovic, which would not be important or relevant except that it is in this case where the Prosecutor turns everything upside down, it is important to say that the Prime Minister was a Croat, Ante Markovic, and that federal government proclaimed these two acts of Slovenia and Croatia unconstitutional on the 26th of June and sent troops of the JNA to Slovenia to restore order on the international border of Yugoslavia, on the low convene side the border of Yugoslavia with Austria and Italy and Hungary. So it was not part of the joint criminal enterprise it was a decision of the federal government and the assembly of the SFRY. Just 2.000 troops were sent to restore order on the international border of Yugoslavia, its sections in Croatia and Slovenia. Already on the next day, the 27th, the Republic of Slovenia attacked units of the Yugoslav People's Army. In the last decade of the 20th century, in the territory of Yugoslavia, secessionist forces mounted an attack against the federal armed forces of Yugoslavia. This resulted in conflict which killed ten Yugoslav soldiers and ended in a cease-fire on the 28th and 29th of June in Slovenia. However, already on the 29th of June, members of the Slovene Territorial Defence continued to attack the JNA, and a general massacre, a general conflict, all-out conflict occurred because very few soldiers were sent to intervene according to the orders of the federal government. The Slovene president, Kucan, appeared as a witness before this Trial Chamber [as interpreted], the man who led this secession, the man who gave the order to attack federal forces, who on the 29th of June declared Slovenia does not give up on its independence, and that was grounds enough for him to attack the federal army. That was a crime. And in that situation, thanks to the intervention of the European Community, some decisions are made and most importantly the decision of the Presidency of Yugoslavia of the 18th of July, in Belgrade, that troops of the JNA would withdraw from the territory of Yugoslavia pending a solution to the Yugoslav crisis. That happened on the 18th of July 1991. And this decision on temporary withdrawal of the JNA is again twisted by the Prosecutor. He says the Yugoslav federation no longer exists, you see. However, on the 7th of July 1991, the European Community intervened and that is when the European troika helped conclude the well-known Brioni agreement that was part after peace plan that envisaged, 1, to cease all actions in Slovenia and, 2, that Slovenia and Croatia should freeze their decisions on independence for a term of three months. So at that moment, it was a demand that looked like an attempt to conduct political negotiations and take a break in the enforcement of certain decisions in order to find a solution to the crisis. What is indicative for the further course of the crisis is that the European Community, when it mediated on the 7th of July 1991, expressed its intention of participating in the Yugoslav crisis but already on the 7th of July demanded that the JNA withdraw to barracks. Your Honours, we are now also dealing with international law, and the laws governing armed conflict, as well as the right of federal authorities to act on their own territories to suppress armed rebellion. As early as the 7th of July 1991, the European Union is asking the JNA to withdraw to barracks where they will be sitting ducks. How else can one explain this demand that they withdraw to barracks while they are being vehemently attacked? In any case, the state leadership of Yugoslavia, on the 18th of July, performed an act of the greatest possible goodwill and withdrew the troops from part of its territory in order to avoid a conflict. General Kadijevic, as the then Minister of Defence, when explaining this action, said the following, and the Defence will show this: "That the military leadership of the federal state was facing a terrible dilemma. In Slovenia, which has a small territory and a small number of inhabitants, should they use brutal military force, use the air force and tanks to suppress the rebellion at cost of enormous casualties, or simply abandon this territory when the Slovene population with its leadership such as it was, was expressing so much hatred toward the federal army? The state leadership of Yugoslavia then decided that they would abandon their own territory if this would be a basis for peace." The Prosecution has submitted a document in which Dr. Wolfgang Pohrt in the magazine Konkret which is published in Hamburg on the 9th of September 1991, speaks of these events. I will quote Mr. Pohrt. On the 9th of September 1991, he wrote, "Instead of intervening decisively and introducing a state of emergency, instead of assaulting the secessionist governments, instead of putting the governments of Slovenia and Croatia on trial for high treason, the federal government ordered its armed forces to carry out a half hearted attack only on the armed forces of the Slovene separatists. This is probably the first time in military history," Dr. Pohrt writes, "that a regular army, that is the JNA, which found itself in a difficult situation, preferred to accept its own losses rather than use its heavy weapons in battle ruthlessly." That's what Dr. Wolfgang Pohrt says, writing in Hamburg on the 9th of September 1991, whereas the Prosecutor, in his indictment, says or construes the sending of federal troops to Slovenia under the command of the Presidency as part of the joint criminal enterprise. One must also bear in mind the fact that the crises in Slovenia and Croatia culminated simultaneously. On the 25th of June 1991, both Slovenia and Croatia enacted decisions on secession. And what the political situation and developments in Yugoslavia showed was that in Yugoslavia, there were forces not seeking a political solution. These were the leaderships of Croatia and Slovenia. They did not want a political solution. They wanted to break up Yugoslavia. The Defence will demonstrate this through the evidence it presents, both live testimony and written documents. However, to understand the behaviour of all the participants in the crisis, one must bear in mind a dramatic fact. On the 1st of July 1991, four or five days after Croatia and Slovenia declared secession from Yugoslavia, the European Community, which was allegedly mediating to resolve the crisis, literally forced the Presidency of Yugoslavia to elect Stjepan Mesic as the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia. There is written evidence of this. The European troika attended the Presidency session of Yugoslavia and this is the first time in modern history that a head of state was elected under the pressure of and in the presence of representatives of foreign powers. The extent to which this was dramatic is demonstrated by the fact that the newly elected president, Stjepan Mesic, such had arrived from a republic which five days previously had already seceded from Yugoslavia. The Croat Mesic from the Republic of Croatia which is seceding is forcibly imposed on the Presidency of Yugoslavia as the president of the Presidency, and this happened at this crucial period in time. The attempts of some political forces in Yugoslavia to oppose this because politically this was completely unacceptable, it was logically unacceptable, it was pragmatically unacceptable, but the Prosecutor portrays this too as part of the joint criminal enterprise. Imagine. Mesic was not elected in the regular way. On the 1st of July 1991, Mesic, who is currently the president of Croatia, was elected to the head of the Presidency and on the 5th of December 1991, when he left that office, stated in the Croatian parliament, and I quote him, "I have carried out my task. Yugoslavia no longer exists." Your Honours, there was evidently another joint criminal enterprise at work, an enterprise to break up a sovereign European state, Yugoslavia. After the Presidency of Yugoslavia issued the decision on withdrawing the JNA from Slovenia on the 18th of July 1991, large JNA convoys with heavy weapons and ammunition, left Slovenia and they had to pass through the territory of Croatia on their way to Belgrade. The Presidency of Yugoslavia was not therefore playing a trick. They were not withdrawing weapons from Slovenia in order to keep them in Croatia, which was already seceding, although they would have had a basis to do this, and a full right to do this, as the federal authorities. No. They didn't do that. But what did the leadership of Croatia do with Tudjman, Mesic and others at its head? They looted the trains. In July and August, these trains were ambushed and dozens of wagons full of weapons and ammunition were looted from the JNA in order to arm paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, let me understand a little point here. Do you say Mesic was the president of Croatia at the time? What was he in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I simply mentioned that Mr. Mesic was a high-ranking HDZ official and a high-ranking official in Croatia at the time. He was the Croatian representative in the Presidency of Yugoslavia. But today, now, he is the president of Croatia. He has been for years. He followed Mr. Tudjman. And I may have mentioned this, and that may have caused the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. To understand the situation in Yugoslavia, it's interesting to note that the European Community, in that period while the JNA was withdrawing from Croatia, condemned the JNA for its military actions in Slovenia. The question arises whether this was official political support to the secessionist aims of Croatia and Slovenia. In any case, the situation on the ground deteriorated and we heard from Prosecution witnesses that all JNA barracks on Croatian territory were besieged. Both in Croatia and in Slovenia and in every other Yugoslav republic, the JNA, as the federal armed force, was deployed and had been for 50 years, in garrisons which had already existed for 50 years in all those places. Your Honours, it was not JNA facilities -- those JNA facilities that were besieged were not new facilities, recently built facilities. It was the depots, warehouses and other facilities that had already been on the territory of that federal unit in a regular way. Their water and electricity were cut off, supplies were cut off, minefields were laid around these barracks, as well as antitank hedgehogs, and there were armed people around every military facility. Armed conflicts broke out, such as the one in Mirkovci on the 22nd of July 1991. This was a conflict between Croatian policemen and local Serb forces, who were also Croatian citizens. There were 12 killed. On the following day after Croatia declared secession, that is on the 26th of June 1991, Croatian policemen took the police station in Glina. From there, they were driven out, after a conflict with local Serb forces, on the 27th of July 1991. On the 1st of August, Franjo Tudjman, in Zagreb, called on the population of Croatia to be prepared for war. He said, "We have to continue preparations for all-out war, if we cannot avoid it." On the 22nd of August 1991, Franjo Tudjman demanded from the Presidency of the SFRY that the army withdraw to barracks. The federal armed force on the territory of Croatia was under attack from all sides. Tudjman was asking that they be closed in, that they become sitting ducks. On the 26th of August 1991, armed conflicts broke out all over Croatia. The fighting around Vukovar began. This was not aggression on Vukovar. It was fighting around Vukovar, in which there were JNA barracks. On the 31st of August 1991, JNA air force planes intercepted a Ugandan airliner bearing 19 tonnes of weapons. They made it land on the JNA military airport in Pleso near Zagreb. These were weapons which Croatian emigres in Canada had bought with money collected among members of the HDZ there. All this was happening during the Brioni moratorium, that is the decision that the decision on secession not be implemented. The European Community was the author of the Brioni document under which Croatia and Slovenia were to suspend their decisions and not carry out them. However, these two republics were active in military terms on their own territories to carry out this decision. On the 3rd of September, under such circumstances, 12 countries of the European Community agreed in The Hague that Lord Carrington, the former British foreign minister, be the coordinator of the peace conference on Yugoslavia on the 3rd of September 1991. On the 3rd of September 1991, however, the German Bundestag supported the thesis that the recognition of Croatia and Slovenia was a road to a faster resolution of the Yugoslav crisis. This was recognition of republics which were teetering on the verge of civil war. On the 7th of September 1991, the international conference on Yugoslavia began its work in The Hague. Under such circumstances of general tension, and uncertainty, the 9th of September 1991 occurred, where Mr. Martic was arrested, and this is again a prime piece of evidence in the view of the Prosecution supporting the case for a joint criminal enterprise, because Mr. Martic was released by other members of the same enterprise, Kadijevic and others. In the situation where the situation in Croatia was already heated, the arrest of Martic could only cause the conflict to spread. So it was quite logical that the federal authorities should exert an effort to release Martic in order to avoid greater damage. However, this is used by the Prosecutor to support his case that there was a joint criminal enterprise. Already on the 13th of September, armed units of Croatia capturing Croatia General Aksentijevic of the JNA. On the 17th of September 1991, Lord Carrington, as chairman of the conference on Yugoslavia, agreed with the federal secretary of National Defence, General Veljko Kadijevic and Croatia's President Tudjman, one of the first cease-fires, the 17th of September 1991. On the 25th September 1991, the UN Security Council adopted a resolution banning imports of arms into Yugoslavia, whereas on the 1st of October 1991, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence submits a report to the effect that from the conclusion of the cease-fire on the 17th September until the 1st of October, that is over a period of 13 days, 263 attacks on JNA installations and units occurred on the territory of Croatia. We have written evidence about this. And since Lord Carrington was appointed chairman of the conference on Yugoslavia, and since he had already been in communication with General Kadijevic, federal minister for defence on the 17th of September, the federal Ministry of Defence introduced the practice that had never existed before or after in the whole world. The most secret documents, daily operative reports received by the Ministry of Defence from the territory of the entire country, were to be submitted every day in writing, including all data, to Lord Carrington, to the Presidency of Yugoslavia, to all presidents of all Yugoslav republics, to the federal executive council, to Mr. Hue tonne, the European Community, that is foreign states, from which assistance is expected in resolving the spiraling Yugoslav crisis. The most confidential military information is provided day to day, about activities, attacks, locations. We will present this evidence, Your Honour, and the Prosecution has it too, and has disclosed copies. These documents do not speak to joint criminal enterprise as the Prosecutor claims, or criminal activities of the JNA or aggression on the part of the JNA. These documents speak to the existence of an armed insurgency on the territory of Croatia, every day and every minute, from August 1991 until the arrival and deployment of UN troops and the final withdrawal of the JNA from the territory of Croatia. It was only on the 3rd of October 1991, while the Brioni moratorium was still in effect and the situation was supposed to be calm, it was only on the 3rd of October 1991 that the Presidency introduced the state of emergency. Let me remind you of one fact that we, as the Defence, will demonstrate. In September 1991, especially after mid-September, in the territory of Croatia, huge JNA barracks were captured, huge barracks, Varazdin, Bjelovar, Krizevci, and other locations throughout Croatia. It is difficult to enumerate all of them now. An enormous amount of weaponry was seized. In certain barracks in Slavonia, 200 tanks were seized in one go. And all this happened while Slovenia and Croatia were bound by the agreement reached with the European Community to freeze their decisions on independence. In that time, Croatia was ruthlessly attacking the federal armed force, and Croatia was preparing in this way to continue the war. Concerning the Brioni moratorium, another thing is typical. Deputy Prime Minister of Croatia, Dr. Zdravko Tomac spoke of the first government of democratic unity in Croatia in August 1991, and he openly writes, as the Deputy Prime Minister of Tudjman's government, saying this: "Because of the Brioni moratorium, we could not form a wartime government. However, we did turn the present government into a Crisis Staff and established a series of other Crisis Staffs throughout Croatia, and thus, on the sly, the Croatian government acted as a wartime government contrary to Brioni agreement," writes Mr. Tomac. And we will lead evidence about this. This activity of the Croatian government had, as its objective, to crush the JNA as an armed force, which in the words of the Deputy Prime Minister of Croatia was done by transferring 17.000 officers and NCOs of Croat ethnicity from the JNA into the new Croatian armed forces. They transferred either voluntarily, of their own will, or, as Dr. Tomac put it, those who did not want to transfer of their own will, even if they did not participate in military actions against Croatia, could not be certain that their lives and the lives of their families would be safe. And Dr. Tomac boasts in his book, "We destroyed the federal army. And we left in the JNA only those cadres through which we could control the situation in the units in which they remained." Whereas the Prosecutor claims that the split and break up of the federal army is another proof of joint criminal enterprise. He says, "You see Croats and Slovenes and Macedonians and Bosnians were all expelled from the JNA." We will demonstrate the contrary, Your Honours, that those officers trampled on their word of honour as officers and they abandoned their own army at a time that was most difficult for it, at a moment when it was their duty to defend the federal state with their lives, if necessary. At that moment, they betrayed it. And the fact that they were no longer part of the JNA seems to be proof in the eyes of the Prosecutor that the army was cleansed on ethnic grounds, purged. Everything in this indictment is turned on its head, Your Honours. And what does the army do in this situation? The army, led by General Kadijevic, was closely cooperating with Lord Carrington and all the other representatives of the international community, and it was under the pressure of the European community that the Yugoslav people's army, in the course of its heavy struggles with Croatian armed formations, concluded a cease-fire on the 2nd of January, the 13th and the 14th cease-fires, the 14th was concluded on the 23rd of November in Geneva. It was signed by General Kadijevic when it was agreed in the presence of Milosevic and Tudjman that for the 14th time around, an attempt should be made to lift the siege of JNA barracks and troops, to allow them to withdraw from the territory of Croatia. That agreement concluded in Geneva is a crown piece of evidence that the Yugoslav People's Army had no ambitions to carry out an aggression, that it was not involved in a joint criminal enterprise, because the army -- an army that agrees, for the sake of peace, to withdraw even from Croatia so that the peace conference on Yugoslavia could find a peaceful solution, an army like that was not part of the joint criminal enterprise, as the Prosecutor claims; without any grounds, in my submission. By doing so, the army, on the contrary, demonstrated that it was not capable, that it did not have the courage, to perform its duty under the constitution to defend its territory, and the resulting gains from those 14 cease-fires were all on the Croatian side, because the Yugoslav army could have easily crushed a resistance had it had the will to do so and we will present written evidence and show through our military expert that the greatest number of JNA soldiers who were killed or wounded were killed or wounded precisely during the cease-fires that were violated by Croatian armed units. Under those circumstances, on the 8th of October, a day after the expiry of the Brioni agreement, the Brioni moratorium that envisaged a pause for Croatia and Slovenia from the 7th of July onwards, the next day after its expiry on the 18th of -- on the 8th of October, the parliament of Croatia takes another step towards secession from Yugoslavia, passing a decision to break away. On the 9th of October, the day after this decision was passed, Mr. Mesic, who was still, let me remind you, president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, a day after Croatia proclaimed its decision to break away and to separate, disassociate itself from Yugoslavia, Stjepan Mesic declared his intention to continue as president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia. And he indeed continued until that day when he declared in the Croatian parliament that his mission is accomplished, that Yugoslavia is no more. At a session of the Croatian state council on the 12th of November, Stjepan Mesic informed President Tudjman and the entire Croatian leadership that as president of Yugoslavia through his own private connections on the island of Korcula on the Adriatic Sea, he had been to see Mr. Andreotti of Italy illegally and at that meeting of the Croatian state council, and that is another document that had been disclosed to us by the Prosecution, Mesic informs Tudjman and the Croatian leadership that Andreotti had promised him that Italy, Austria and Germany would recognise the Croatian and Slovenian independence even if the European community fails to do so. At that meeting, Mesic also says, cynically, and just imagine, I went there, allegedly, as head of the Yugoslav state. That speaks volumes about the ethics of the man who gave a solemn oath when he became president of the Presidency of the Yugoslav state. These may be scandalous and tickling facts but on top of that, Mesic says that Andreotti told him on that occasion, "Lord Carrington informed me that president of Serbia Milosevic had told him that he doesn't need a yard of land to create greater Serbia. He's only interested in the rights of Serbs in Croatia. And after hearing this, Mesic informs Tudjman, "I explained to him that Milosevic was not telling the truth. He wants to preserve Yugoslavia for purposes of greater Serbia." Why am I explaining this, Your Honour? Those separatist forces that broke up Yugoslavia were falsely accusing at the same time those Yugoslav republics, like Serbia, who were trying to save that federal state, who were loyal to the federal state, and to falsely accuse it, they used the fiction of greater Serbia. The OTP had abandoned that fiction of greater Serbia in another case, the case against Milosevic, saying that they had never advocated that theory. On the 8th of October 1991, thus, Croatia proclaimed its decision to sever all links with Yugoslavia and on the 16th of October, Croatia gave a deadline to the JNA to withdraw from the territory of Croatia. Croatia demands from the Yugoslav People's Army, "Withdraw from our territory." At that time, the conflicts are well under way and on the 17th of October 1991, in The Hague, Lord Carrington proposed a declaration on independence of all Yugoslav republics that wish independence. It was at an international conference, where all the principles of the OSCE and international laws that hold the international identity of states as something sacred, at an international conference, sovereignty and independence is offered to all those who wish it. Imagine if something like that would be done for Catalonia, the Basque country, anywhere in the world. And still, that really happened for the territory of Yugoslavia. When on the 17th of October, the federal authorities rejected this document, another version was offered to them. Another version was created by the European Community and then a third version of such a document. On the 1st of November, 1991, the Presidency of Yugoslavia pointed out that the document was unacceptable and that it was not the solution. On the 4th of November 1991, the council of ministers of the European Community adopted a package of restrictive measures envisioning punishing those Yugoslav republics who did not agree to the break-up of the state. These were the political events that took place. But they are linked to the Prosecution case about the so-called joint criminal enterprise, and the possible intentions of some sides in Yugoslavia. There are written documents according to which the European Community, for reasons the Defence will demonstrate, supported the secession of certain republics, and these are the facts. From the very first document proposed by Lord Carrington on the solution of the Yugoslav crisis, on the 17th of October 1991, until the 8th of November 1991, a very brief time elapsed, yet the Defence will show what happened in that time period. On the 8th of November 1991, the European Union decided to impose sanctions on those disobedient Yugoslav republics which did not agree to the break-up of Yugoslavia. Instead of imposing sanctions on the secessionist republics, Croatia and Slovenia, on the 8th of November the European Union imposed sanctions on Serbia and Montenegro because they opposed the document that was on offer. This was the political environment in which certain events took place on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. On very next day the 9th of November 1991, Yugoslavia appealed to the United Nations, that is the Presidency of Yugoslavia, asking that the UN send troops to the territory of the former Yugoslavia so that a peaceful solution could be found. On the 9th of November 1991, the presidency of Yugoslavia sought UN intervention to protect the integrity of Yugoslavia. As early as the 23rd of November 1991, Cyrus Vance, the special envoy of the Secretary-General of the United Nations reached an agreement in Geneva with Veljko Kadijevic, Tudjman and Milosevic on a cease-fire and the lifting of the siege on all besieged JNA units on the territory of Croatia, as well as the lifting of the siege on all the garrisons of the JNA in Croatia, which would enable the JNA to withdraw from Croatian territory. This agreement, reached in Geneva on the 23rd of November 1991, was the basis for the UN resolution on the peacekeeping operation of the UN in Croatia and this was adopted in February and is known under the name of the Vance Plan. Therefore, the military and political leadership of Yugoslavia expressed its goodwill on the 23rd of November 1991 in Geneva to do everything possible to prevent war, even withdraw their own forces from part of its own territory. However, the Prosecution accuses that military leadership in this indictment of participating in a joint criminal enterprise with a view to expelling non-Serbs from one-third of Croatian territory. This is truly incredible. On the 27th of November 1991, only 15 days after the Yugoslav government submitted a request to the UN to send the blue helmets to Yugoslavia, resolution 721 was adopted by the Security Council on the urgent deployment of UN troops in Yugoslavia. On the 9th of December 1991, a month later, the Presidency of the SFRY told Lord Carrington that the decisions of the arbitration commission were unacceptable because they would mean the collapse of Yugoslavia as a state, its being taken off the map. We will draw attention once again to S23, 280, of the 11th of December 1991, a document issued by the Secretary-General of the United Nations in which he tells the Security Council and the European Community that under the conditions of the planned arrival of UN troops in the former Yugoslavia, a premature recognition of particular Yugoslav republics would be disastrous for the region. Along with this document, S/23280, of the Security Council in 1991, there is a letter to Mr. Van den Broek, sent to him by the Secretary-General, on the 10th of December 1991, in which he draws the European community's attention to the fact that a premature recognition would simply be pouring oil onto the flames and that the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of Macedonia and other Yugoslav republics were asking that this not be done, but it was done. It was done on the 23rd of December 1991, when first Germany recognised Croatia and Slovenia. It was done on the 13th of January 1992, when the Vatican recognised Croatia and Slovenia, and on the 15th of January 1992 when other countries of the European Union recognised Croatia and Slovenia in opposition to the request by the Secretary-General. The Defence will show that before this recognition, the president of the USA, George Bush, senior, in a conversation with the secretary -- with Perez de Cuellar of the United Nations, pointed out that it would be unacceptable to prematurely recognise the independence of particular Yugoslav republics which were seeking recognition. Why is the Defence drawing attention to these events? Because these facts have been neglected by the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor overlooks them as if they didn't exist. Yet they show in what political environment the Yugoslav crisis was taking place and the circumstances in which the actions of all the participants in that crisis took place, including Mr. Martic and other participants of the alleged joint criminal enterprise. On the 8th of December 1991, in Zagreb, under the auspices of the European Community, this was about a fortnight after the Geneva agreement of the 23rd of November 1991, under the auspices of Vance, an agreement was reached between the Croatian government and the JNA on the withdrawal of the JNA from the territory of Croatia, the entire territory of Croatia. Whereas the Prosecutor states that the JNA, which was under attack on Croatia, the fact that it was there is evidence of a joint criminal enterprise. This agreement on the withdrawal of the JNA on the 8th of December was the 15th agreement of this kind, Your Honours, mediated by the European community and it was not respected because Croatian forces continued fiercely attacking the JNA. Logical evidence to support what I say, and this is also conceded by the Prosecutor, is that on the 2nd of January 1992, a peace agreement was signed in Sarajevo. On the 23rd of November in 1991, there was an agreement in Geneva, under the auspices of Vance, that the JNA withdraw, and then again on the 8th of December another agreement contravened by Croatia, and finally on the 2nd of January 1992 in Sarajevo an agreement was signed on withdrawal which would enable UN troops to arrive on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. In the meantime before the end of 1991, in these political circumstances, another event transpired that is linked to the content of the indictment: The republic of Serb Krajina was prom you will gated on the 19th of December 1991, a constitution was adopted, and the Republic of Serb Krajina was established as the state of the Serb people who had previously lived on the territory of the Republic of Croatia which was now seceding and abandoning Yugoslavia. The Croatian people were recognised their right to secede. The Serb people in Croatia was only asking for the same right. They were far smaller, far weaker, amounting to only 12 per cent of the population, but they did not want to leave their state. They wanted to remain within the Republic of Serb Krajina. In these political circumstances, when many key players of the international order were working on the break-up of Yugoslavia, is being used by the Prosecutor as evidence to support the thesis of a joint criminal enterprise. Everyone in Yugoslavia, the Macedonians, the Croats, the Slovenes, the Muslims, they all had the right to self-determination. Only the Serbs did not have that right. How generous the Prosecutor is! In connection with this peace mission of the UN in Yugoslavia, a prerequisite was that there be a cease-fire. We have already seen what documents in January show that these conditions had not been met. There was no cease-fire in place yet. We have seen Security Council documents saying that the JNA is withdrawing from Croatia but there is no cease-fire yet. The last cease-fire was signed in January 1992 and this was followed by events closely linked to the indictment. Mr. Babic, Mr. Milan Babic, the president of the RSK, and the government of the RSK, adopted the position that UN troops could arrive on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, that this was useful, but they made two demands, that the troops be deployed on the demarcation line between Serb and Croat forces. That is on the borders of the RSK facing Croatia. Is this illogical? Is this unreasonable? That had been the practice before in every peacekeeping mission, both in Cyprus and everywhere else. UN troops were always deployed on the demarcation line separating the two sides. That's what Mr. Babic was asking. He was asking one other thing, that JNA troops not withdraw from territory of the Krajina. Mr. Babic explained this to Mr. Marek Goulding and this was a meeting held in Knin on the 27th of January and he did not desist from his demands because according to the then standpoint of Mr. Babic, it was up to international factors and Yugoslavia whether they would withdraw the JNA from Croatia, but he was asking that they remain on the territory of the RSK Krajina to protect the Serb population there. On the 8th of January, because of Mr. Babic's standpoint on the arrival of UNPROFOR which was contrary to the plan which envisioned the deployment of these troops all over the territory of the Krajina and the withdrawal of the JNA from the territory of the Krajina as well, on the 8th of January, the president of Serbia, Milosevic, wrote an open letter publicly condemning Babic, and calling him to account. Mr. Babic replied to that letter on the 12th of January. On the 30th of January, in Belgrade, a meeting was held of the extended Presidency of Yugoslavia. In addition to the members of the Presidency, representatives of the Serbs from the Krajina and those in Bosnia who recognised the federal state attended the session which lasted until the 31st of January and the 1st and 2nd of February 1992. A communique was issued stating that the Yugoslav side, the state of Yugoslavia, as the party requesting the arrival of UN troops agreed to the deployment of those troops and guaranteed that the troops would in fact be deployed as agreed. They also promised that Yugoslavia would comply with its obligations. At that meeting, the agreement of the Serbs from Croatia was also obtained. This was done by Mr. Milan Paspalj; Mr. Babic did not attend that meeting. In connection with this meeting, the Presidency of Yugoslavia informed the Security Council that UN troops would be there to protect the Krajina Serbs should, for any reason, or rather that the JNA would protect the local Serbs should the UN fail to do so. This calmed the fears of the local Serb population. This meeting was held in Belgrade which was their capital town in their own country, but again, this is seen by the Prosecutor as evidence of a joint criminal enterprise. They say, well, look here, they went to Belgrade. What do the Serbs of Krajina, what business have they to go to Belgrade? But, Your Honours, only the state of Yugoslavia was legally in existence at the time, and at the invitation of the president of their state, the Serbs went to Belgrade to accept the Vance Plan. And even regardless of that, let me not go into what the Prosecutor believes is the end date of Yugoslavia, the motivation, the reason for this meeting, was to accept the deployment of UN troops and the UN plan. Even that is used by the Prosecution as evidence of the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. That is absurd. The absurd is complete. And we had to point out one more thing about Mr. Babic. As to his view that UN troops must be deployed along the demarcation lines and that the JNA should stay in Krajina to protect the local population, Mr. Babic explained why he believed that, why he insisted on that, even to international representatives, and over this point, he clashed with the most influential Serb politician at the time, Mr. Milosevic. We heard that he may have been a very ambitious man, but it's important to know why he took the risk of clashing with Milosevic. And as we saw later, he may have been right. The Serbs were not protected by UN troops. There were five aggressive operations against the Serbs from the Croatian side ending with Operations Flash and Storm, in which 250 to 300.000 Serbs from expelled from Croatia with only 50.000 remaining. Out of 581.000 that were there in the census of 1991, after the military operations of the Croatian army, only 50.000 remained. And under these circumstances the Prosecutor speaks of a Serb joint criminal enterprise. Mr. Babic had good reason to insist on his standpoint that he presented in September as well. We put to him that letter in which he wrote at the time that the JNA was acting in a decent, regular way, that the Serbs in Krajina were only asking for the same rights as the Croat population has, and that is to decide their own fates. And the reason for all the trouble was the conduct of the neo-Nazi new Croatian authorities. Everything that Mr. Babic did at the time was reasonable, logical and was justified by later developments. Nothing can deny these facts. On the 14th of -- sorry, on the 4th of February 1992, in New York, after the Presidency of Yugoslavia declared on the 3rd of February that it would accept the Vance Plan, Boutros Boutros-Ghali declared that Croatian laws would not apply in UN safe areas in Yugoslavia, in Croatia. This was stated by Mr. Marek Goulding on behalf of the United Nations Security Council. On the 14th of May, the Presidency of Yugoslavia proclaimed an edict whereby the legal system of Yugoslavia would apply to the parts of Yugoslavia that are under special protection of the United Nations. So it was also the standpoint the United Nations and the decision of the Yugoslav federal state that the areas in which UN troops were deployed were areas of Yugoslavia, where Yugoslav legislation applies. And that legislation did apply, and it was enforced in all the decisions of the Republic of Serb Krajina. Since on the 3rd of February 1992, the Presidency of Yugoslavia elicited the consent of the RSK, the assembly in Glina passed the necessary decision to accept that plan and Mr. Borislav Jovic, as president of the state committee for cooperation with the United Nations, informed the United Nations thereof and this is another official document of the Security Council. At that meeting in Glina, on the 9th of February 1992, Mr. Martic was present. He too supported the Vance Plan. There were also the vice-president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, Branko Kostic, and Blagoje Adzic, acting Minister of Defence. Their presence in Glina, in order to secure acceptance of the UN plan, is also used by the OTP as evidence of joint criminal enterprise: "Look, people from the state authorities came to visit those renegade Serbs." Then the Security Council of the United Nations adopted resolution 743 concerning UN protected areas in Yugoslavia and Mr. Babic was replaced as president of the RSK because he was -- he would not agree to the Vance Plan. On the 26th of February 1992, a new president of the RSK was elected. On the 29th of February 1992, in Bosnia, another Yugoslav republic, a Croat-Muslim referendum was held concerning the independence of this republic without a participation of Serbs. The indictment also refers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go on to that one, can we perhaps take a break, Mr. Milovancevic? Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, how much longer are you likely still to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
