utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's difficult to evaluate because I'm trying to speak moderately slowly for the benefit of the interpreters. When I write it seems to me that it would be shorter but I suppose that tomorrow, during the first session, I'll be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic, just that -- sorry, yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask if I could just have five or ten minutes at the end of the session today, as I mentioned earlier I had a few housekeeping matters to raise and I would like to raise them today. I thought that the opening would be finished today so if I could have five or ten minutes at the end of the day, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic, can you spare Mr. Whiting some five to ten minutes at the end of the day, just to do some housekeeping matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I'll make sure. Towards the end of the previous session we mentioned that the process of acceptance of the Vance Plan by Yugoslav participants was finalised with the decision of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Borovo Selo to replace the president of RSK, Mr. Babic, from his post precisely because he was opposed to the Vance Plan. As regards the allegations in the indictment related to Bosnia-Herzegovina, we received some evidence during the Prosecution case that emphasised the problems and the situation prevailing there, but the Defence would like to point out once again that the approach of the Prosecution is very lopsided and selective. Two or three locations, two or three townships are chosen in a large territory and then, by viewing certain events in isolation, conclusions are drawn about the situation in the whole region and even worse, conclusions are made about the existence of a joint criminal enterprise that encompassed Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. The Defence will lead evidence to show that in this period in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the period of the indictment, starting with end February 1992, and I will remind Your Honours that one of the Prosecution witnesses, Mr. Kirudja told us that in April, early April 1992, when he arrived in the former Yugoslavia, the situation was calm and peaceful. Whether this was just an appearance or the truth, we will show through the evidence we lead. As regards Bosnia and Herzegovina, in December 1992, the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina addressed the Secretary-General of the United Nations, and he speaks about that in his document dated 11th December 1991, that premature recognition should not be granted to certain Yugoslav republics. However, that premature recognition was granted despite all the warnings, and it is important in view of the Prosecution case to explain why and how this was done. On the 29th of February 1992, a referendum was held of two ethnic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslim and the Croat communities. The Yugoslav republic, Bosnia-Herzegovina, was particularly well known as a republic that had three constituent ethnic groups, Muslims, Croats and Serbs. Those three nations were autochthonous and formed the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina for many centuries back. The constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina defined this republic as a union of these three constituent nations and it was defined in the same way in the constitution of Yugoslavia. Only peoples had sovereignty, had sovereign status, as opposed to national minorities. Considering that Bosnia and Herzegovina was a republic where three communities divided by religion and ethnicity were living together, it was very important to preserve that balance and to give equal treatment to those three ethnic communities to avoid conflict. In order to understand the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a federal unit of Yugoslavia, I will just say briefly that during the Second World War, Bosnia and Herzegovina was a part of the so-called Independent State of Croatia, the Ustasha state of Croatia. On the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, inhabitants of Serb ethnicity suffered a horrific genocide, and now, on the 29th of February 1992, with the crisis in Yugoslavia unfolding as it was, and after the Security Council already passed a resolution to send UN troops to Yugoslavia to be deployed in areas of Croatia where Serbs formed a significant majority of the population, and where interethnic strife or rather tension had in the past led to conflict, in that situation, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a referendum is suddenly organised for two ethnic communities, Croats and Muslims, against the third ethnic community, the Serbs. The same question arises as in Croatia and Slovenia: Will Bosnia and Herzegovina become independent and will it continue as part of Yugoslavia? This referendum on the 29th of February 1992 was held at a moment when the Security Council of the United Nations had already decided in its resolution on the Vance Plan and all Yugoslav parties had undertook to enable the JNA to withdraw from Croatia, including the territory of Krajina, from areas that would be protected by the United Nations. So at the moment when the Security Council is making its decision on this peacekeeping operation, and the Yugoslav People's Army accepts to pull out from Croatia, Bosnia is a part of Yugoslav territory, which has a long border with Croatia, and under those circumstances, the decision to pull the JNA out of Croatia practically meant that they had to move to Bosnia and Herzegovina, which borders Croatia. From its own territory, from Yugoslav territory, of which Bosnia and Herzegovina was a part, it was indeed easy to intervene militarily in case the Serb population in Croatia is attacked. However, political events at that point took a completely different turn. On the 29th of February 1992, this referendum is held and two nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims and Croats, decided that Bosnia would secede from Yugoslavia. Serbs hold their own referendum and said, "We will stay in Yugoslavia." And then a political crisis breaks out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the international community intervenes, the United Nations, and the European community intervene. The events in Bosnia looked ominous. The referendum was on the 29th of February and already in March that year, a terrible incident occurred in Sarajevo. It is very important, if we want to understand the situation in Bosnia, to note that this population was completely mixed. There were no purely Croat areas, purely Serb areas or purely Muslim areas. No. The population had lived together for many centuries and after their experience of World War II, they still continued to live together. In old Yugoslavia, the Yugoslavia that existed until then, it was very frequently said that Bosnia was an example, a paragon of brotherhood and unity, three nations and three religions together. However, at the time when the situation in Croatia was still unresolved, the UN troops were still not deployed and the JNA had not withdrawn, in the centre of Sarajevo Muslim forces killed one Nikola Gardovic and warned a Serb Orthodox priest. This Nikola Gardovic was the father of the groom in the wedding party. The Serb flag carried by the wedding party was seized and burned. This is an individual crime, Your Honours, and crimes happen. However, this particular crime caused terrible unrest in all of Bosnia, and disorders began in the streets of Sarajevo because of this. On the 18th of March 1992, 19 days later, under the aegis of the European Community negotiations on the fate and the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina begin in Lisbon. Representatives of three main political parties, the Muslim party, SDA, Party of Democratic Action led by Alija Izetbegovic, the Serb Democratic Party led by Radovan Karadzic, and the Croatian Democratic Union from Bosnia, meet in Lisbon under the chairmanship of the president of the European Community, Mr. Cutileiro, and arrive at what we know as the Cutileiro plan to resolve the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to that plan, all these three parties, the Muslim, Serb and Croat ones, and representatives of the three ethnic communities, agreed that a future Bosnia would be organised along cantonal principles, would have three constituent units and according to the maps that were offered, Muslims would get 44 per cent of the territory, Croats 12 per cent and the Serb population would get 44 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That plan, sponsored by the European Community, had as its objective to save Bosnia from war. The Defence will show that only section days later, on the 25th of March 1992, spurred by the American Ambassador in Belgrade, Warren Zimmermann, the leader of Bosnian Muslims, Alija Izetbegovic, reneged on this plan and withdrew his signature. Already on the 26th of March, after this political turnabout, Croat and Muslim forces, in village Sijekovac [phoen] near Bosanski Brod, slaughtered 21 civilians of Serb ethnicity. Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina reacted by holding their own assembly meeting and adopt the first constitution of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The political response of the Muslim leadership in BH was the decision of the 4th of April proclaiming mobilisation of the Territorial Defence in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina as forces loyal to the new leadership bent on secession. Just after that, on the 6th of April 1992, contrary to the warnings of the Secretary-General of the United Nations, the European Community recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent and sovereign state, using as a basis the referendum held by two Bosnian nations without the third one on the 29th of February 1992. The next day, the 7th of April, the United States recognised Bosnia too. The Serb population and Serb political parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina respond on the 7th of April by proclaiming Republika Srpska, at a meeting of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We have now reached the 7th of April 1992. Your Honours, this is a period when a high-ranking official of the UN, Mr. Kirudja, arrived on the territory and said that the Bosnian situation was still peaceful. After that, events spiraled into a disaster. As Bosnia was recognised on the 6th and 7th of April by certain states, the status of the JNA was suddenly at issue. Up to the 6th of April 1992, the JNA in Bosnia had been on its own territory. The JNA status in Bosnia was characterised by the fact that this was the central republic geographically speaking, and it was a mountainous area. And for these strategic reasons, the chief military facilities, the main weapons depots, the most important airports, such as the one in Bihac, an underground airport in the mountains, the most important military factories were all located in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina was a disaster for that army because it was left without its military industry, its most important depots and warehouses, but in spite of all that, on the 26th of April 1992, as the Defence will show, negotiations were held in Skopje between General Blagoje Adzic, the chief of the General Staff of the JNA, and the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic. This was on the 26th of April 1992, when Bosnia was already recognised by some countries, which does not necessarily mean it was already an independent state but the survival of the JNA was at stake. An agreement was then reached between Alija Izetbegovic and the top of the JNA, that the JNA should peacefully withdraw from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The main problem had been solved. According to that agreement, there was no reason for war. Only three days later, however, in spite of this agreement, which he signed with the JNA on the 26th of April, Alija Izetbegovic and his leadership issued an order on the 29th of April 1992 on complete and large-scale obstruction of all roads used by the JNA to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Secondly, to lay siege to all military facilities in BH. Thirdly, to prevent JNA units from leaving the barracks from which they were meant to withdraw. And fourthly, to urgently start military operations against the JNA on the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your Honours, somebody wanted war and disaster, and it happened, but this was not a Serb joint criminal enterprise, as the Prosecutor claims. After this decision of the 29th of April 1992, there was widespread armed conflict all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Defence will present documents, operative reports, from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. These were documents such as those sent to the Presidency of Yugoslavia, the presidents of the republics, The Hague Conference, and other international bodies and they related to Bosnia-Herzegovina. The JNA, however, continued withdrawing from Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 3rd of May 1992 with the mediation and presence of UNPROFOR, that is in the presence of the Canadian General Lewis MacKenzie and Carl [as interpreted] Doyle, an emissary of the European Community the command of the 2nd JNA army in Sarajevo signed an agreement with Alija Izetbegovic that it should peacefully withdraw from Sarajevo. Armed conflicts had already begun, but according to this agreement, mediated by Mr. MacKenzie and Mr. Doyle a peaceful evacuation was agreed upon. General MacKenzie was in the JNA convoy which was then suddenly attacked in the centre of Sarajevo and JNA soldiers were killed. The UNPROFOR general was witness to a terrible crime by which the JNA was betrayed on this occasion. Responding to this event, this massacre in the centre of Sarajevo, on the 4th of May 1992, the Presidency of Yugoslavia decided that all members of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina who were citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should return to the territory of Yugoslavia within 15 days. So this removes any dilemma as to whether the political top leadership of Yugoslavia was in favour or not in favour of the withdrawal. This was a public call to withdraw. On the 15th of May 1992, the Security Council of the UN adopted resolution 752 to cease fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for there to be a cessation of fighting, but on that same day in Tuzla in the north of Bosnia a JNA convoy which was leaving Tuzla was attacked. More than 200 out of 600 soldiers were killed. This was done by paramilitary Muslim units. This was a slaughterhouse. In spite of this kind of behaviour, on the 22nd of May 1992, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia and Slovenia were received as members of the United Nations as sovereign member states. In Bosnia, there was an armed conflict ongoing. In Croatia, UNPROFOR was not yet deployed. And there were still conflicts. The JNA had left Slovenia. But these three states were received into the United Nations. All this was done at a time when UN troops had not completed their deployment in Yugoslavia and the UN resolution envisaged UN troops securing peace so that a peaceful solution to the crisis in Yugoslavia could be found at an overall level. Now, suddenly, the UN Security Council is receiving three member states from the former Yugoslavia into the United Nations. The manner of this receipt into membership is also interesting. The cause and effect is very important. These three secessionist republics were admitted following a strong media campaign at a session chaired by Mr. Peter Hornfeller [phoen]. The proposal was unusually brief, consisting of only one sentence, without entering into the actual situation. The UN Charter in Article 2, paragraph 1, provides that sovereign states may be members of the UN. So this was the assumption when these three states were admitted by acclamation in a brief procedure. So far the procedure had always been respected and 35 days had always elapsed from the application to the admission. However, this was not done. The president of Saudi Arabia, Samir Shihabi, in the United Nations, referred to his brothers in faith, the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and demanded that the JNA swiftly withdraw, and these are the circumstances in which these three republics were admitted. This defined the future course of developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there is much evidence to support it. A propaganda war, Your Honours, the disinformation, the way public opinion is manipulated, all these are methods of warfare. The crisis in Yugoslavia involved an incredible amount of deception and trickery. On the 27th of May 1992 in the center of Sarajevo in a well-known street, Vase Miskina street, a shell exploded in a street where there was a bread line, and this was a reason for the Muslim delegation to interrupt negotiations in Lisbon on the future status of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnia had already been admitted no the United Nations but the representatives of the three constituent peoples were still discussing peaceful coexistence in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This terrible explosion took place on the 27th of May 1992. On the 23rd of August 1992, only two months later, based on an inspection of confidential UNPROFOR reports received by commander Satish Nambiar, a reporter of the Independent paper from New York, revealed that several of the most horrendous massacres in Sarajevo, including the murder of 16 civilians in the bread line were perpetrated by Muslims in order to win over public opinion for a military intervention and that this was not done by the Serbs who were accused of these crimes. That's what the independent published on the 23rd of August 1992. However, the political consequences were already there. Negotiations on the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina were interrupted and after this interruption, and the massacre in Sarajevo the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 757 imposing a strict and comprehensive regime of sanctions on Yugoslavia. On the 30th of May 1992, the Security Council felt it was Yugoslavia that was responsible for what was happening on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Only three days later, however, the international press reported on a shock experienced in New York because the Secretary-General of the UN, Boutros-Ghali, had prepared a report on the 30th of May 1992, the date when the resolution on the condemnation of Yugoslavia was passed, but this report was concealed and published with a two-day delay, only after one side in Yugoslavia, the federal state, had sanctions imposed on it. It was only then that the report was published although it was already in existence when sanctions were imposed, and according to this report, the Serb forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina are outside Belgrade's control. He reported that they were completely out of Belgrade's control. Also, he reported that the reason the JNA had not withdrawn from Bosnia-Herzegovina was actually the siege and the blockade carried out by Alija Izetbegovic's forces. Thirdly, he mentions in the report that there is Croatian aggression in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is very important to assess the so-called Corridor Operation with which Mr. Martic is also being charged by the Prosecutor. The Secretary-General reported that there were Croatian troops on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas the Prosecutor claims that Operation Corridor was an attempt to create a greater Serbia rather than cutting off the only route that could possibly be used by the aggressors from another state, from Croatia. On the 15th of June 1992, a new president of Yugoslavia, Dobrica Cosic was elected. This is interesting only because after this date, the Presidency of the SFRY no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment, please, Mr. Milovancevic. Sorry to interrupt you. I need to confer with the learned Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please, this interruption is regretted but I feel compelled to speak at this point. The purpose of the opening is very, very specific, as you might know. I myself have held back because I had hoped at some point you would become more focused and we would learn precisely what the case that you are relying on for the Defence would be, and the evidence that you intend to lead before the Trial Chamber. Up to this point, I regret to say I'm able to distinguish between your commentary, your personal commentary, between your historical background and I am able -- not able, rather, at this point, to ascertain through your own words what is the evidence that you intend to lead. The Trial Chamber -- and I believe I can speak on behalf of my learned brothers because I took the liberty of consulting them before speaking -- the Trial Chamber should not be left in a mystery and state of confusion as to what evidence you hope to lead. So I know that my learned brother, the President, had sought to redirect you and to get you to focus but you have to so articulate what you have to say, that we understand what it commentary by you and what is the evidence that you hope to lead in support of your case. I don't think I can put it any clearer than that and I hope that this will guide you in but please do get to what is the purpose of the opening statement, that the Defence is entitled to make, with expedition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the methodological approach that the Defence has chosen is something I will try to explain very briefly now. We have submitted a list of the evidence we intend to call during the presentation of our case. These are all United Nations documents, documents issued by the federal authorities, and the 65 ter exhibits submitted to the Defence by the Prosecution. The Defence has selected this approach in an attempt to deny the fundamental case of the Prosecutor. That is that there is a joint criminal enterprise. By presenting the chronology of events on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, we hope to refute the conclusion by the Prosecutor that on the territory that the indictment refers to, the events took the course described by the Prosecution. We wish to present to the Chamber a chronology of events. This is borne out by open-source documents. The question is should the Defence point to particular documents at this stage? The Defence has documents to support all this. At this point in time, the Defence felt it important to provide a summary which would show that events took quite a different course from that presented by the Prosecution, that the Prosecution has presented only a twisted, out-of-context representation of the events. The Defence is attempting to show that one cannot skip over certain events and fail to create the linkage, that one cannot reach conclusions on the basis of an isolated segment of these events. If the Chamber wishes my statement to be focused on the charges in the indictment, I'm aware of the problem, Your Honours, but the problem is in the indictment, because it is based on claims concerning a political programme, which is not borne out by a single document. The Prosecutor even goes to far as to say there is no need to prove this because events on the ground can demonstrate that this alleged joint criminal enterprise and its plan existed. This can be refuted by simply presenting a chronology of the events as they took place and pointing to the relevant documents which bear them out. Of course, I will comply with your instructions, Your Honours, and thank you for drawing my attention to the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I just wish to say further that you know at this stage what the counts are in the indictment. I would think also you know at this stage what the several issues that you have to respond to in your defence are, and I really would have anticipated that in relation to those two factors, your articulation of the Defence case would have been more specifically related to those two factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. Do you require any further explanation or response from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Not unless you consider it absolutely essential but I think I've put it to you with as much clarity as I can. I do wish to be assisted by you and I honestly felt that I wasn't feeling comfortable with the manner with which it was dealt with and if I could assist you to put me in a greater level of comfort together with my brothers then it would assist the business of this Tribunal very, very greatly, Mr. Milovancevic, and please accept it in that spirit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I wish to provide some further explanation by your leave which will lead into what I will present next. The facts on the ground, the crime base, as it is called, is something that the Defence will deal with in its specifics through witness testimony. At this stage of the proceedings, the Defence only wished, and I do take on board what Your Honour has told me, but I would like the Chamber to understand what the Defence case is. In the view of the Defence, what is most important now is to refute the thesis about a joint criminal enterprise. In the indictment the Prosecutor gives a list of participants. The entire political, military and police leadership of the then Yugoslavia and particular republics over a five year period. Without providing any explanation as to what, how and why they were doing, except for what happened on the ground, and then they draw a conclusion from what happened on the ground that there was a joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution case of joint criminal enterprise involves a political plan which was implemented over a five year period. The Defence wishes to draw the Chamber's attention to all the key political events in that five-year period which go to show something quite different. These are the facts we have been mentioning now, and through its witnesses, and expert witnesses, the Defence will demonstrate this. It should not be a big problem for the Defence to deal with the crime base, but it's very important to establish whether the joint criminal enterprise existed or not. This political programme at work in the former Yugoslavia at the time. This is a political thesis. It's a thesis about a political programme, and a political goal, which fails to correspond to the real events on the ground. The Defence is not attempting to defend improper behaviour on one side by pointing to improper behaviour on the other side. That would certainly not be acceptable. But we feel that we cannot establish what actually happened unless we establish what the political events were. We have not received a single document or piece of evidence from the Prosecution about how this joint criminal enterprise was carried out except for perhaps what was done by one company in Skabrnja or one battalion in Saborsko. There were only several hundred men involved in those cases but that is not the entire JNA. That is not the entire police or the state or Yugoslavia, whereas the Prosecutor says it is. It is very difficult to refute this kind of indictment in any other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess, Mr. Milovancevic, the point that is being made is that we understand that the Defence position is to refute the existence of the joint criminal enterprise but I think what is expected in an opening is for you to say, "We, the Defence, submit that there was no joint criminal enterprise, and we are going to lead evidence to establish that." And not for you to take the whole day giving us evidence on how the joint criminal enterprise does not exist. I said to you in the first session, I'm getting the impression you are testifying. And in the second and in this last session, this third session, I'm now convinced you are testifying. All what you have been telling us, it would build up your case better if you told us that through your witnesses. You have put the thesis, your theory up front, "My theory of my case is there was no joint criminal enterprise." That's the theory. Having told us that you sit down and you call your witnesses to come and testify and show us that there was no joint criminal enterprise. Not for you to tell us this whole history. Let us get this history through your witnesses, Mr. Milovancevic. I think this is really what we are asking you to do. You are not a witness in this case. You are counsel. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you're saying, Your Honour. Thank you very much. What the Defence believed to be important is this and I'll try to be very brief and of course I will follow your instructions. By pointing out the chronology of events, we wanted to justify the leading of some evidence through live witnesses and documents. Through the opening statement, it was my idea to present the principal arguments of the Defence rather than to testify. But in line with your instructions, allow me to proceed. Do I have your leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have all the leave, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have just pointed out, Your Honour, the Defence is going to try to show in its case that not a single element of the charges in the indictment, legal or factual, stand. There was no plan and no organised activity aimed at expelling population, creating inhumane conditions, detaining people, killing people. There was no plan to cause conflict with Croatian armed forces in order to ultimately involve the JNA, to implement any kind of joint criminal enterprise by fighting in villages and driving the population out. The Defence will present documents to show that it was a conflict with armed secession -- against armed secession, an attempt to deal with protracted sieges laid to military barracks. The Defence will show that the Republic of Croatia illegally imported arms, illegally armed civilians, and formed illegal armed forces. We will show that through documents, including the documents of the Ministry of Defence. We will show that in villages and towns that were peaceful until then, wartime units were created, including in Saborsko and in Skabrnja and in seven villages surrounding Skabrnja and Bacin, Dubica. The Defence will show that it was distribution of weapons to the population led by the political party under the leadership of the political leaders of Croatia, weapons were distributed to one ethnic group only, the Croat population, whose illegal formations were active, and the Defence will show that in all these three locations, Skabrnja, Saborsko, and Kostajnica, as we will designate them, in all three locations, the places concerned were extremely important to the JNA and its positions, seven villages together with Skabrnja formed a large military airfield. The Defence will show that illegal paramilitary formations were equipped with uniforms imported from East Germany, with automatic rifles, that the federal army clashed with these units by necessity, out of necessity. The Defence will show through its military expert that the conduct of these military operations had nothing to do with any joint criminal enterprise, nor any objectives alleged in the indictment, that they were aimed at lifting the siege of military barracks and opening up the communications that were blocked in that area. The Defence will show that all the units involved in combat activities acted in keeping with the federal legislation, that the principle of singleness of command was being implemented, that all units were united under the same command, the command of the largest unit leading the operation, and such was the case in both Skabrnja and Saborsko. The Defence will call witnesses to show that the events in all these locations that formed the crime base have nothing to do with the militia of Krajina or Martic's Police. We will show through the documents of Krajina that there was in existence a regular police force, the police of Krajina whose work was regulated by law, that there were regular prisons under the control of the Ministry of Justice, that people who administered these prisons were employees of the Ministry of Justice. Under the then Yugoslav and Croatian legislation, prison staff did not belong with the police force or the Ministry of the Interior. The Defence will further show that the protracted pressure that Serb people were subjected to in the territory of Krajina and the whole of Croatia eventually led them to organise themselves. The Defence will lead evidence about the conduct of the highest authorities of Croatia, to show that the leadership of Croatia, led by President Tudjman even back in 1991, operated with the fact that it needed to get rid of Serbs in certain professions and areas. Only 6 per cent of the personnel of the MUP who were Serbs were left in 1992, as opposed to a much larger percentage before the HDZ started its activities. It was an organised and massive dismissal of Serbs from various positions. There was no plan on the Serb side. It was an attempt to use armed force to discipline the Serb population of Croatia. People were dismissed, killed, intimidated, their houses bombed. And in all that, all these horrible tensions and conflicts led to a complete breakdown of the system. The state was no longer able to function. Interpersonal relations deteriorated. The basest instincts took over, on all sides. Through the documents of the UN Security Council, the Defence will show that all the principal elements of a civil war were present in the region. We will show that all that the indictment refers to was happening on the territory protected by the United Nations in the presence of the United Nations under their control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? Mr. Whiting had asked for a couple of minutes to do some housekeeping matters before we knock off today. Would it be a convenient moment to take that time and you can carry on with your opening tomorrow? Is that -- would that be okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Perfectly. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to raise a few matters. The first is that pursuant to the Court's order of last week we did receive yesterday copies of Defence exhibits that we had not had previously. The ones without the ERNs, and we received two binders of exhibits. Unfortunately none of them are translated. So we've received two binders of exhibits in B/C/S or virtually all of them are in B/C/S. I think -- I think a fair reading of the rules requires that -- certainly to be admitted into court they would need to be translated and they are not much use to us. I mean, we have to go through them with an interpreter now. I think we should receive translations of them. I understand from the Defence that they've requested them. I just would ask that that be provided to us as soon as possible because I think that's part of the rules. The second point is the Prosecution's concern that there has been reference to a number of documents, both today and earlier, that seem -- that are described as going to be part of the Defence case and yet do not appear on the exhibit list. For example, during the 98 bis submission, the Defence counsel suggested that he had a photograph of Ambassador Galbraith which he wanted to tender during the argument but certainly made clear that it would be tendered during the Defence case, I think he said on several occasions, in fact. That photograph does not -- that article, that photograph, does not appear on the Defence Exhibit list and we would like to have a copy of it. There have been a number of articles and documents today that have been referred to, an article from Der Spiegel from 1990, a statement or article from Dr. Wolfgang Pohrt from the 9th of September 1991. A UN document from the 11th of December 1991. A letter from the Secretary-General from the 10th of September 1991. UN Resolution 752. And as far as I can tell, I mean, I was doing this while listening but as far as I can tell none of those appear on the Defence Exhibit list. It seems if they are in the Defence opening and they are anticipating using them in the Defence case, they should appear on the Defence exhibit list and I'm concerned about that. The third point is we did receive yesterday two detailed 65 ter summaries or I should say more detailed for the witness who is to start tomorrow and the witness to start after the break. The witness after the break is Momir Bulatovic, and it's listed in the 65 ter summary as being ten hours which is approximately by my calculation three days, even a little less than three days but now the Defence has indicated to us that it will take most of the week and that it's the only witness they can tell us about for that first week. So we are a little concerned about that. We are also a little concerned or would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, what is the actual concern? I didn't catch the nub of the concern on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The nub of the concern is that originally the Defence had indicated that that would be a witness who would take three days and now they are indicating most of the week and it is the only witness they have told us about for that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which week is this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The week after the break. The only issue well one issue I should say with respect to the 65 ter summaries is that I note that with both of them, there is nothing said about what the witness will say, if anything, about Milan Martic. Now, perhaps the witnesses won't say anything about Milan Martic. That's possible. But certainly, if the witness -- if it's expected that the witness will say something about the accused, Milan Martic, that is something that we would expect should fairly be in the 65 ter summary. I note also that for the witness for this week, although the witness is described as being the minister for foreign affairs of the RSK from October 1992 on, from October 1992 on, virtually all of the testimony that he's expected to give and that is described is from 1990 and 1991. It's not clear to me, at least from the 65 ter summary what the basis is for him to be able to give such testimony but perhaps that's something that will become clear during the testimony itself. The final point I wanted to raise, Your Honour, is that we had expected to receive yesterday the exhibits that would be used certainly with the witness who is to start tomorrow but also I think for the witnesses who are to start after the break. We have not received those -- any indication about which exhibits will be used. We received an e-mail saying that we would receive it first thing this morning, today. I think we are well beyond first thing this morning and we have not received anything. So those are the points, Your Honour, I wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic, I hope -- can you please respond to these concerns? Let's take them one by one. Mr. Whiting, if I've miscaptured your concerns, you will have to help me. I've got six concerns that I've noted down. The first one, Mr. Milovancevic, let's deal with that one first. Copies of exhibits that have been received are in B/C/S and they need to be translated, both for the record and the -- they are useless to the Prosecution without a translation. Would you like to respond to that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all that my learned friend Mr. Whiting said is completely understandable, and I understand his position. However, the problem of the Defence is that we are very much pressed for time. We have an enormous problem with time. We only started preparing the Defence case after the Prosecution case was completed, and that's a problem that we tried to point out to the Trial Chamber. I hope that you don't think that the Defence is trying to obstruct the work of the Prosecution. Of course, it is our duty to have this translated but, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not only your duty to have it translated, Mr. Milovancevic, it's also your duty to have it translated timeously. You keep going back to this point that you only started preparing the Defence case after the closure of the Prosecution case. It cannot be acceptable, Mr. Milovancevic. You come to court and you cross-examine Prosecution witnesses, you see the case is going to an end, you simultaneously with that, after hours, you prepare your case, ready to start immediately after the Prosecution case, and part of that preparation includes having translated documents that you intend to use in court when you start your case. The official languages of the Court are English and French and if those documents are not in either of those languages at least you could have them translated. That does not have to be done by you personally. You just assign that job to the translator, to somebody else there, while you carry on with the cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses and doing other professional things. Now, I really cannot understand why you keep saying the Defence case was only prepared after the close of the Prosecution case. I find it very difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence is trying to say actually to the Trial Chamber and to our friends from the Prosecution is that we are facing mission impossible. You cannot ask the impossible of the Defence. You were present at the 65 ter meeting in November, last November, when we said that until that point we had been without any resources for work for 20 months and that we had -- that we were waiting for a decision on our submissions to the earlier trial Chamber and the registry. You were surprised but you still scheduled the beginning of trial for the 13th of December. And we were ready to prepare for cross-examination as we go along. Of course, it's not possible not to work for 20 months. But preparation for cross-examination is one thing. It's easier. Preparing your own case is much more difficult and all that is ahead of us, we know what we have to do and what the rules require and still we are trying to say to the Trial Chamber that we are facing impossible deadlines. And from the moment the trial was scheduled to begin, we have been subject to impossible time pressures and now after this break, we have really got an impossible mission. For each of these stages, the Prosecution had lots more time. He had two months to prepare his opening statement, two months to prepare their list of exhibits and list of witnesses. We know all that. But the work itself is of such volume that we are not coping. We have the reports from experts that have been organised in time but we haven't been able to read it and we could not start preparing our case before the Prosecutor completed his. And all these lists that we had to submit according to 65 ter that we now have to amend by Friday, that has not been done, not because we have no respect for the OTP or because we are ignoring the orders of the court but we are working in circumstances that are impossible. We physically cannot cope. We are working 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When can we expect translations of these copies of exhibits that are in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to consult with other members of my team and then I will be able to tell you. I cannot answer this question now. Why am I saying this? Because the witness whom we are supposed to hear tomorrow arrived last night and we had no contact with him. He just arrived last night. We couldn't see him today because we have this morning's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I don't see how the two connect. Can you consult with your team and let us know first thing tomorrow morning when you think you can give us translations of these exhibits? The next -- I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do so, Your Honour. Sorry, sorry to interrupt. I didn't mean to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The next point that the Prosecution raised, which is a concern to them, according to what I've noted down, is that there are documents that have not been disclosed but are being mentioned in the opening and thereby suggesting that these documents are going to be used, and a whole list of examples was given. The one that I remember immediately is the photograph of Mr. Galbraith. There are a few others that were mentioned. I hope you do understand that for you to be able to use those documents in evidence, you must have disclosed them. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We completely understand and we accept that as our duty, as our responsibility. The photograph of Mr. Galbraith that we did not include is just -- just shows to how much pressure we are subject at this moment. We have thousands of pages of documents, we don't know what to have translated first but we have been in this situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you don't translate a photograph. A photograph is a photograph. It's in a photo language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I meant, Your Honour. I meant to say that it was simply an omission. We omitted to put it on the list because it is -- although it is one of the important documents and it is in our interest to show it, of course we will. It just goes to show under what circumstances we are working now. I hope you can understand our position, after five and a half months of work of the Prosecution, we were preparing for cross-examination as we went along and now, when we could get some rest and go on holiday, we are already tired, we have to use that holiday to work some more. We are not happy to have submitted this list of exhibits the way it is. We made the shortest summary possible, and the Prosecutor is completely right but that's not because we do not respect the work of the OTP or the Trial Chamber. It's because we are working under impossible conditions. The Defence does not have enough time to do everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you, Mr. Milovancevic. When do you think we could have those documents that have not been disclosed and the Defence intends to use in evidence? I think let's -- the idea is to try and solve the problem. When do you think we can have those documents? Or when the Prosecution can have those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my colleague Mr. Whiting is completely right. He mentioned several times that I mentioned in my opening statement. It's a fact they are not on the list and it's our failure, our mistake, but until this moment we were not aware of that failure because of the tempo in which we are working and because it would have been necessary to find exactly what we need out of tens of thousands of pages. Well, I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you once again. Are you able to tell us when you think you can disclose those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence wishes to fulfil its obligations fully, without any need for the Prosecutor to raise any objections. We had no objections to the summary the Prosecutor gave us. It included everything the Prosecutor felt was relevant. If Your Honour can give us a deadline by the 14th of August, we will prepare everything the way it should be done. We must do that. But these short deadlines being given to us now do not assist us to solve this problem, because we are simply at a loss as to what to do first. The Defence strategy is to challenge the fundamental thesis of joint criminal enterprise. This has to be done in the same time that the Prosecutor had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we listen to one another? We are not dealing with the strategy of the Defence at the moment. We are dealing with the documents that are intended for use during the trial which have not been disclosed. We are just trying to find out when the Defence thinks they would be in a position to disclose those documents. Let's stay focused on the issue at hand and try to resolve that issue. You indicated that if the Chamber give you a deadline of the 14th of August you will have done everything that needs to be done and you will have done it properly. Before I revert to Mr. Whiting to find out what he says about your suggested deadline of the 14th of August, let me find out this: In that deadline, you do not include any documents that you intend using this week because the documents that you intend using this week should be with the Prosecution by now, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would propose is that if the Defence -- it's fine for the Defence to have till the 14th of August to come up with a kind of final definitive, as best they can, list by then. However, having said that, it seems to me that the items that I mentioned or any other documents which are present to them that they know now, having prepared the opening and starting to prepare the case they are going to use, they could provide to us this week. In other words I'm proposing a kind of rolling disclosure or submission by the Defence. I would be interested in getting at least those documents and then, if they want to add, to -- add further documents and provide it on the 14th of August, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to give a rolling disclosure, Mr. Milovancevic? At lease those documents you have been mentioning now during your opening, are you able to give them sometime this week? And then during the recess, you can make sure that the remaining documents are processed and are disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I said today we of course should be able to do this by the end of this week. Today, yes, the documents can be disclosed successively until the end of the week, those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you very much. It's so ordered, then. Mr. Whiting, the one -- the next point that I made a note of, you said that you received yesterday more detailed 65 ter summaries but I didn't pick up what the problem was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There were just two concerns. The first is that the Chamber had ordered the Defence to disclose detailed 65 ter summaries for all of the witnesses who would be called during the first week after the recess and we received only one for that week, one witness, who was only supposed to take three days according to the Defence estimation. And then the second point with respect to the summaries is that there is no mention in the summaries of anything that the witnesses, these two witnesses, will say about the accused and as I said perhaps there will be nothing but it just is something I wanted to flag up that in our view the summaries, if the witness is going to say something about the accused, that should be included in the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those are the two issues that Mr. Whiting raises about the 65 ter summaries received, Mr. Milovancevic. Do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as we have done these summaries, I know exactly what Mr. Whiting is saying and I know what his problem is. I understand it completely. With respect to these summaries, the problem of the Defence is very clear. There is a large number of witnesses. We have reduced the list considerably but this again has to do with the trial schedule. The summaries we are redoing now we are again doing under time pressure which causes us to miss things, to have a text that is incomplete or too brief. We know what a witness summary statement should contain, but our physical capabilities are limited. We were very much concerned to hand over this list, the statements are quite extensive. We have been doing that over the past few days but we had many other obligations in parallel, the 98 bis and everything else that followed. What I'm trying to say is that we are working under enormous pressure of time and we simply do not have time to prepare the case in the way we would wish. Our aim is both for the Prosecutor and for ourselves to be able to do our jobs properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, can I interrupt you again? We are all working under enormous pressure here. You're not the only one; if you have only realised that, then welcome to the club. Let me say this: The issue that -- if I understand it well that Mr. Whiting is raising is this: That you have given one witness to testify in the first week after recess. That witness, according to your own estimation, which still is subject to review by the Chamber, is supposed to testify for three days. Now, it doesn't -- that doesn't seem clear whether now, the witness you have given, is he going to occupy the entire week after the term or is he only going to be three days? And if it's going to be three days only, then you've got to give a summary of the other witness who is going to occupy the remainder of that week before we go on recess, if I understand the problem from the Prosecution. And the next point is, none of the summaries that you have given of the witnesses that are about to testify says anything about the accused and he says he understands there may very he will be nothing to say about the accused by these witnesses. However, he's just saying if indeed something is going to be said by these witnesses about the accused, then the Prosecution is entitled to know what that is. Have I captured your concerns correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. So just address those issues and tell us how to get over them. We understand you are working under pressure and we have sympathy for that but just tell us how we should deal with those two issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have considered the testimony of this witness, Mr. Bulatovic, who will come after the recess, and in our estimation, his examination-in-chief should last three to three and a half days, due to the number of documents we wish to tender through him. Therefore, with cross-examination and questions by the Chamber, the witness might take up the entire week. That's why his is the only statement we submitted. Our estimation of course places an obligation on us, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Already, he's likely to take even more than the time you've estimated for him? Do I understand you to be saying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, because our assessment of his testimony, the first one, was based on his statement but now when we revisited it and looked at the documents to be tendered, we see that this is substantial testimony. He was the president of Montenegro. He was the Yugoslav Prime Minister. He was an active participant in these conferences and he will also testify to the acts and conduct of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a difficulty. Judge Nosworthy is supposed to sit at quarter past 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that. Maybe we can bracket this one and finish discussing this one tomorrow. The -- if I could just get an indication of when we are going to get the list of exhibits that are going to be used with the witness who is starting tomorrow, a list that we were supposed to get yesterday, then I would be satisfied --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can you help with that, Mr. Milovancevic, quickly, before we knock off?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will do this urgently by e-mail because of course we cannot begin the direction -- the direct examination unless the materials are disclosed. We shall do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is as soon as possible? How soon is as soon as possible, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to consult the Defence team assistant, Your Honour. I cannot give you the precise time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you happy with that? Okay. Can I put you on terms? Can I say that you deliver that before 4.00 this afternoon, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please don't give us a time limit. If we can, we will do it even before that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
